questions.q: Name the year the Civil Disobedience Movement was launched and the specific act of defiance that marked its beginning.
questions.a: The Civil Disobedience Movement was launched in 1930 with the Salt March (Dandi March), where Gandhi and 78 followers marched 240 miles to make salt from seawater, violating the British salt monopoly. A wrong answer (e.g., 1920 or 1942) shows confusion with the Non-Cooperation or Quit India Movements, indicating the student has not anchored the timeline correctly.

questions.q: Why did rich peasants like the Patidars of Gujarat and Jats of Uttar Pradesh initially join the Civil Disobedience Movement but later become reluctant to participate in its second phase (1932–34)?
questions.a: Rich peasants joined initially because the Depression crashed cash crop prices, making revenue payments impossible; they saw the movement as a no-revenue campaign. They withdrew later because the movement turned toward radical demands (like no-rent) that threatened their own status as landlords, and the Gandhi-Irwin Pact (1931) offered no concrete relief. A wrong answer that says "they lost interest" misses the economic and class calculus — students must link material conditions to political strategy.

questions.q: A factory worker in Bombay participates in the 1930 strike but refuses to join the 1932 phase. Using the concept of "selective participation," explain this shift with two specific reasons.
questions.a: Workers struck in 1930 against low wages and long hours, seeing Congress as an ally; but by 1932, Congress leaders (many from the business class) opposed radical labor demands, and the Communist-led Girni Kamgar Union was banned, leaving workers without leadership. A wrong answer that blames "British repression alone" ignores the internal class tensions within the nationalist movement — a key board exam trap.

questions.q: Compare the participation of women in the Civil Disobedience Movement with their role in the Non-Cooperation Movement. Identify two continuities and one significant change.
questions.a: Continuities: women joined processions, picketed liquor/foreign cloth shops, and spun khadi in both movements. Change: in Civil Disobedience, women from respectable middle-class families (like Sarojini Naidu, Kamaladevi Chattopadhyay) entered public politics in unprecedented numbers, breaking purdah barriers more visibly than in 1920–22. A wrong answer that says "women did the same things" misses the qualitative shift in social acceptance — boards often ask for "change and continuity."

questions.q: Evaluate the statement: "The Civil Disobedience Movement failed to become a truly mass movement because the Congress did not address the specific demands of Dalits and Muslims." Support your judgment with two pieces of evidence.
questions.a: The statement is largely valid. Evidence 1: Ambedkar demanded separate electorates for Dalits at the Round Table Conferences; Gandhi’s fast unto death forced the Poona Pact (1932), which gave reserved seats but not separate electorates, alienating Dalit leaders. Evidence 2: Muslim participation dropped sharply after 1930 because the Congress rejected the 14 Points of Jinnah and the movement’s Hindu symbolism (e.g., Ramrajya) made Muslims wary. A wrong answer that says "everyone joined" ignores the structural exclusions that boards test via case-based questions.

questions.q: Construct a timeline (1930–1934) showing five key events that illustrate the widening and narrowing of participation in the Civil Disobedience Movement. Annotate each event with the social group most affected.
questions.a: A strong timeline includes: (1) March 1930 – Salt March begins (peasants, women, students); (2) May 1930 – Gandhi arrested, mass protests erupt (industrial workers in Sholapur, Peshawar); (3) March 1931 – Gandhi-Irwin Pact signed (business groups withdraw support); (4) September 1931 – Second Round Table Conference fails (Muslims, Dalits disillusioned); (5) January 1932 – Movement resumes, but Congress banned, leaders jailed (participation collapses). A poor answer lists events without linking them to social groups — boards require "annotated" timelines.
